blocks.text: 1. Checkpointing

blocks.alt: Model state saved to disk becomes a checkpoint

blocks.text: Validation Loops, the previous topic, measured performance without touching the weights. Checkpointing covers how to save a network's progress during training, a genuinely essential practical safeguard explored throughout this topic.
It works by writing weights, and other training state, to disk at meaningful points, preserving progress that would otherwise be genuinely lost if training were interrupted.
2. Why Checkpointing Is Genuinely Necessary

blocks.alt: Training crashes without a checkpoint lose all progress

blocks.text: A genuinely real, practical risk motivates this entire topic. Training can run for genuinely many hours or days, already covered in Epochs, especially for genuinely large networks and datasets.
Crashes, power loss, or timeouts can genuinely destroy hours of progress instantly, a genuinely real, practical risk that Checkpointing exists specifically to protect against.
3. What Actually Gets Saved

blocks.alt: A checkpoint saves model weights, optimizer state, and epoch number

blocks.text: This connects back to weights, already covered throughout Backpropagation & Optimization. The network's weights are the genuinely essential minimum to save, since they represent everything the network has learned so far.

Optimizer state, current epoch, and hyperparameters are also commonly saved alongside them, already covered individually in earlier topics, giving a genuinely complete picture of the training run at that exact saved moment.

blocks.text: 4. When Checkpoints Typically Get Saved

blocks.alt: At the end of each epoch a checkpoint gets saved

blocks.text: This connects back to the outer loop, already covered in Training Loops. Checkpointing typically happens once per epoch, right after the validation loop finishes, already covered in the previous topic.
This is a genuinely natural point where a complete, coherent training state exists, with that epoch's training and validation both already fully processed before the checkpoint gets written.
5. Best-Model Checkpointing

blocks.alt: When validation improves, a new best checkpoint gets saved

blocks.text: This connects back to validation loss, already covered in both Learning Curves and Validation Loops. A genuinely common strategy saves a checkpoint only when validation loss genuinely improves over the best seen so far.

This ensures the genuinely best-performing version of the network is always available, not just the most recent one, protecting against the exact overfitting pattern already covered in Learning Curves where later epochs can genuinely get worse.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Best-model checkpointing directly connects to the overfitting pattern already covered in Learning Curves, where validation loss can start rising even as training loss keeps falling. This strategy protects against exactly that risk.

blocks.text: 6. The Connection To Early Stopping

blocks.alt: Early stopping restores the best checkpoint

blocks.text: This connects back to Early Stopping, already covered in the Regularization Techniques module. When training stops early, the best checkpoint, already covered in this topic, is what actually gets used going forward.

This is a genuinely direct, practical dependency between these two concepts, since Early Stopping's own value depends entirely on having a genuinely saved, best-performing checkpoint available to actually load afterward.
7. Resuming Interrupted Training

blocks.alt: Interrupted training loads a checkpoint and resumes where it left off

blocks.text: A genuinely valuable practical benefit follows. This connects back to the crashes and interruptions already covered earlier in this topic. A saved checkpoint lets training resume from that exact saved point.
This happens rather than starting over from scratch, saving genuinely significant time and computational cost whenever an interruption occurs partway through a genuinely long training run.
8. Overwriting Versus Versioning Checkpoints

A genuinely important practical tradeoff arises here. Overwriting the same checkpoint file each time saves disk space, but loses every earlier saved state, keeping only the genuinely most recent one available.

Keeping multiple, separately versioned checkpoints uses genuinely more disk space, but preserves a genuinely fuller history to choose from, a real, practical tradeoff between storage cost and flexibility.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Checkpointing Is Genuinely Essential

Training genuinely long-running, expensive jobs, already covered, is a direct case for Checkpointing, since its ability to resume, already covered in this topic, directly protects against genuinely costly lost progress.
Wanting to keep the genuinely best-performing model, not just the final one, is another genuine case where best-model checkpointing, already covered, directly delivers this.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a genuinely simple best-model checkpointing strategy, saving a snapshot only when validation loss genuinely improves.

code.content:
import numpy as np

# Simulating validation loss across epochs, already covered in Learning Curves
val_losses = [0.85, 0.62, 0.51, 0.48, 0.53, 0.49, 0.55]

best_val_loss = float("inf")
best_epoch = -1
checkpoints_saved = 0

for epoch, val_loss in enumerate(val_losses, start=1):
    print(f"Epoch {epoch}: validation loss = {val_loss:.3f}")
    if val_loss < best_val_loss:  # best-model checkpointing, already covered in this topic
        best_val_loss = val_loss
        best_epoch = epoch
        checkpoints_saved += 1
        print(f"  -> New best model, saving checkpoint (checkpoint #{checkpoints_saved})")

print(f"\nBest checkpoint: epoch {best_epoch}, validation loss = {best_val_loss:.3f}")
print(f"Total checkpoints saved: {checkpoints_saved}, already covered as best-model checkpointing in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows checkpoints being saved only at epochs 1 through 4, since validation loss starts rising at epoch 5, exactly the overfitting pattern already covered as the motivation for best-model checkpointing.

blocks.text: 11. Training Deep Networks: Progress Recap

items: Checkpointing saves a network's weights and training state to disk at meaningful points during training.
It protects against lost progress from crashes, power loss, or timeouts during long training runs.
A checkpoint typically includes weights, optimizer state, current epoch, and hyperparameters.
Checkpoints commonly get saved once per epoch, right after the validation loop finishes.
Best-model checkpointing saves a checkpoint only when validation loss genuinely improves.
Early Stopping directly depends on the best checkpoint being available to load afterward.
Checkpoints let interrupted training resume from a saved point, avoiding a costly restart from scratch.
Overwriting versus versioning checkpoints trades off disk usage against preserved history.
